newsitem.title: NIGERIA: FEATURE - Museum thieves steal Nigeria's heritage.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Museum thieves steal Nigeria's heritage.

text.p: Thieves are emptying Nigerian museums of valuable antiquities, with officials blaming demand from Europe for a new trend that is depriving the country of the symbols of its past.
In the past year at least eight of the nation's 30 museums have been looted.
"Our country has become a major source of illegal trafficking in antiquities," said Yaro Gella, director of the National Commission for Museums and Monuments (NCMM) in Lagos.
Most of the objects were smuggled across the country's land borders to European destinations, he said.

For decades Nigerian museums had been repositories for the country's wealth of antiquities, including bronze figures and tools, wooden masks, carved ceremonial and ritual objects and other artefacts produced centuries ago.
NIGERIAN ARTEFACTS FETCH BIG PRICES ABROAD
All that has changed as the high prices fetched by such objects abroad have become common knowledge.

The Niger State museum in north central Nigeria last year lost works dating back 300 years or more, valued at over $46,000, including terra cotta items and a ritual smoking pipe of the Kafinkor ethnic group, alone valued at $15,000.

Thieves who raided the National Museum, Esie, also in central Nigeria in January last year drugged the museum guards before making off with famous carvings said by experts to be one of the biggest collections of stone sculptures in Africa.
Early this year the museum at Oron in southeastern Nigeria lost 36 objects, while another at Ife, in the southwest, lost 34 - all within a space of a few weeks.
"Thieves have looted the Ife Museum three times in the past four years and some of the works ended up in France," said Helen Kerri, assistant director for museums and monuments at NCMM.

"We found out that the thieves, especially those that burgled the Owo, Ife and Jos museums, went for specific objects. So it gives us the impression that they are well informed about the value of the objects," she said.
SHRINES ARE NOT SPARED BY THIEVES
Apart from museums, traditional shrines have also been raided in recent times and carved images of gods taken away for illegal export.
A major incentive for the illegal trade is that Nigerian artefacts are among the most valued of African antiquities.

The Ife and Benin bronzes of western Nigeria and Igbo-Ukwu bronzes of the east are world famous. So is the 2000-year-old Nok terra cotta found in the central Plateau region, one of the earliest such remains found anywhere in the world.

In the 1950s and 1960s, tin-mining activities in the plateau yielded archaeological finds, particularly the Nok terra cottas. Now illegal miners are turning their attention to archeological finds which are sent abroad for handsome cash rewards.
POLICE FOCUS ON ILLEGAL TRAFFICKING IN ARTEFACTS

Ibrahim Coomassie, Nigeria's police chief, told a meeting of West African police chiefs in Abidjan last July that ..."103 precious artefacts have been stolen from our museums and 88 are on sale in the Netherlands and Spain."
"They were taken out of Nigeria by road, mostly through the countries of the West Africa sub-region."
At a follow-up meeting of the same police chiefs in Abuja, Nigeria a few weeks ago, the illegal traffic in antiquities was among other regional crime issues of growing concern discussed.

According to NCMM's Kerri, the illegal international traffic in Nigerian (and African) antiquities is sustained largely by the refusal of the major European powers to sign and ratify the 1970 UNESCO Convention on Restitution of Cultural Property.
"Britain right now, for instance, is an active receiver of stolen artefacts from Nigeria, and we are very worried because this encourages their theft," she said.
NIGERIANS EAGER TO EXPORT ANTIQUITIES FOR MONEY
If Western countries are willing to receive, some Nigerians are eager to part with their antiquities.
An antique shop in Lagos popular with expatriates is now a major depot for various artefacts making their way to metropolitan Lagos from the rural areas.
Although export of antiquities is illegal in Nigeria, other traditional artefacts considered to be mere copies of originals can be taken out of the country with permits issued by NCMM.
This blurs the line between genuine antiquities and copies, making possible to export of the former as the latter.

"We receive an average of six applications daily for export permits from foreign visitors and expatriates wishing to take artefacts out of Nigeria," said an official of NCMM, adding "Sometimes there are as many as 10 applications, with each person sometimes seeking to export as many as 30 objects."
NIGERIA MOVES TO RECOVER ARTEFACTS ABROAD
The ministry of information and culture recently set up a committee charged with recovering Nigeria's stolen artefacts.

NCMM says this is the first step in evolving a new cultural policy whereby ..."Our cultural heritage is left where they should be and foreigners are encouraged to come and study our culture here, if they so desire," instead of taking them away.
